To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cold gas accretion can explain the low V /σ observed in massive disks and that the porosity model allows for efficient formation of massive galaxies.

cold accretion can increase the number of massive star-forming galaxies at z ∼ 1.5 − 3, and the porosity-based star formation prescription can increase the star formation efficiencies to the level needed to reproduce the observed number densities and the mass functions of galaxies at these redshifts.

cold accretion can explain the puzzling low V /σ in disk galaxies at z = 0, and that the star formation rate in the universe is consistent with the observed star formation rate density, if cold accretion also drives turbulence in disks.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the formation and evolution of galaxies, and in particular with the role that accretion plays in the star formation history of galaxies.
the formation and evolution of the most massive galaxies in the early universe.
the following issues: (i) The origin of cold gas flows and their role in the formation and evolution of galaxies. (ii) The formation of massive disks and their evolution to massive ellipticals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the observed star formation rate density in the universe at z = 1.2 − 2.2 is in the range of ˙ ρ * = 0.01 − 0.02 M ⊙ yr Mpc −3.
the star-forming galaxies at z = 1.4 − 2.5 have properties that can be explained in the context of hierarchical galaxy formation models.
cold accretion flows are the main driver for star formation in massive disk galaxies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the cold accretion flow model is able to reproduce the observed properties of the massive star-forming galaxies at z ∼ 1.5 − 2.5, if we allow for a large fraction of accretion energy to drive turbulence in gas disks, and a high efficiency of star formation.
the star-forming main sequence at z = 0 is not the same as at high redshift, and that the evolution of the main sequence is not monotonic, but rather shows a peak at intermediate redshifts.
we can reproduce the observed number density of massive galaxies at z = 3, if we allow a fraction of 18 % of accretion energy to drive turbulence in the gaseous disks.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cold accretion can provide the gas supply for the formation of massive galaxies at high redshifts and that the porosity model is a viable mechanism for the conversion of gas into stars.

cold accretion, in combination with the porosity model for star formation, can reproduce the observed properties of star-forming galaxies at z ∼ 1.4 − 2.5, including the number densities, the mass functions, and the low velocity dispersions in massive disk-like galaxies.
the star formation history of the universe is strongly affected by the interplay between cold flows and the porosity of the interstellar medium.
